articles.title_orig: Don't Let China's Espionage Become America's Own Goal | Blogs | Nov 12, 2026 - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.title_zh: Don't Let China's Espionage Become America's Own Goal | Blogs | Nov 12, 2026 - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.content_orig:
An alleged Chinese intelligence operation targeting Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang could end up costing the United States far more than it costs China. Nvidia has lost its longtime chief executive, American investors have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and U.S. policymakers are considering new restrictions on chip exports that could further undermine American technology companies. The United States has a legitimate interest in preventing the Chinese military from acquiring advanced AI chips, but it should not allow an alleged Chinese espionage operation to push it toward policies that weaken its own semiconductor industry.
The controversy began with reports that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, of working for China's Ministry of State Security. Investigators reportedly suspected she had cultivated a relationship with Jensen Huang to gather information about Nvidia and its operations. Jensen Huang acknowledged having an extramarital relationship with her and separately faced reports of another relationship with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. On November 12, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO after 33 years leading the company and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
The allegations raise serious national security concerns. Megaspeed reportedly purchased approximately $4.8 billion in Nvidia hardware . U.S. authorities suspected that the company was helping Chinese customers circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips. During a 2024 inspection of a Malaysian facility, Commerce Department officials reportedly found Nvidia hardware still packed in boxes rather than installed in data centers, raising concerns that the equipment might be destined for China.
These allegations remain under investigation. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing, says it is cooperating with inspections by U.S. authorities, and has commissioned an independent review by a U.S. law firm of its chip inventory and export-control practices. Singaporean authorities are also investigating the company.
If the allegations are true, China will have achieved something significant: disrupting one of America's most important technology companies and potentially gaining access to sensitive commercial information. Even without evidence that Nvidia's trade secrets or national security information were compromised, the damage is already substantial. Nvidia has lost its longtime leader, its shareholders have seen hundreds of billions of dollars in market value evaporate, and the company faces renewed uncertainty about its ability to serve international customers. The immediate economic costs are falling on an American company and its investors.
China's own semiconductor strategy makes the situation particularly revealing. Beijing wants to reduce dependence on American technology and build a domestic chip industry. It has increasingly used procurement restrictions and government guidance to steer Chinese companies toward domestic processors. In November 2025, for example, Chinese authorities reportedly directed state-funded data centers to use domestically produced AI chips . In January 2026, Chinese authorities also discouraged purchases of Nvidia's H200 processors, despite strong interest from Chinese companies.
Yet Chinese companies continue to seek access to Nvidia's most powerful processors, including through overseas data centers. This reflects a distinction between Beijing's long-term industrial ambitions and the immediate commercial interests of Chinese technology companies. China wants its domestic chipmakers to capture the market, but its AI developers still benefit from access to the best available hardware.
Congress now risks helping China achieve its goals. One proposal, the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) , would expand export controls to cover foreign access to restricted U.S. technology through cloud computing services. The legislation addresses a legitimate concern: Chinese companies could potentially rent computing capacity overseas even when they cannot legally purchase the underlying chips. But an overly broad law could also create uncertainty for legitimate international cloud services and impose new compliance costs on American technology companies.
The AI OVERWATCH Act and Chip Security Act would go further. The AI OVERWATCH Act would require licenses for certain advanced-chip exports to countries of concern and give Congress advance notice of proposed sales, with an opportunity to block them through a joint resolution. That process could make access to U.S. chips subject to greater political uncertainty, even for transactions that meet existing export-control requirements. The Chip Security Act would require security mechanisms to help verify whether exported chips have been diverted, potentially including location trackers, on-site audits, or legal attestations. Such measures could help detect illicit transfers, but they could also raise concerns among legitimate international customers about monitoring, data security, and government access to information about their computing infrastructure. Both bills risk making U.S. technology less attractive to customers who have other options.
The United States should strengthen enforcement against companies and individuals that knowingly divert restricted chips. It should also improve verification of end users and investigate suspicious transactions. But Congress should be careful about creating new restrictions that unnecessarily limit legitimate commercial activity.
American semiconductor leadership depends heavily on private-sector investment in research and development. Nvidia and other U.S. chipmakers spend billions developing successive generations of increasingly powerful processors. International sales generate revenue that supports this investment, helps companies achieve economies of scale, and finances future innovation. Overly restricting access to the Chinese market would weaken an important source of commercial demand while giving Chinese competitors more opportunities to improve their products and gain market share.
China has an obvious interest in reducing its dependence on American semiconductors. But its own record of economic espionage and trade-secret theft—including documented efforts to steal semiconductor technology —underscores why the allegations deserve serious attention. President Trump should put the issue on the agenda when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month.
Any proven violations should carry meaningful consequences. But a domestic response that hurts American companies, reduces their global markets, and encourages customers to adopt Chinese alternatives would compound the damage. China may have played Jensen Huang. Congress should make sure it does not play into Beijing's hands.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at Kalshi prediction market
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at Kalshi prediction market
articles.content_orig:
Prediction market platform Kalshi ended its advisory contract with Donald Trump Jr. in response to his venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, also holding a stake in rival platform Polymarket, according to Kalshi's spokesperson.
Conversations on Trump Jr.'s exit began in August after 1789 Capital announced a major stake in Polymarket , the spokesperson said. It was a mutual arrangement, with both Kalshi and Trump Jr. agreeing it was a conflict of interest to keep the president's son as an advisor while serving as a top investor for Polymarket, the spokesperson added.
Trump Jr.'s departure comes after Democrats secured a majority across the House and the Senate, with the party expected to crack down on the prediction market industry. While Trump Jr. has exited Kalshi, he still serves as an advisor to Polymarket. His ties to the industry could make prediction markets an easy target for lawmakers to go after, Joseph Konizeski, a former trial attorney in the CFTC, previously told CNBC.
In early October, Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said on MS NOW that Trump Jr.'s connection to the company creates an "optics issue," but added that it has never relied on that relationship to gain favor with the government.
Kalshi first named Donald Trump Jr. a strategic advisor for the company in January 2025.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_orig: US envoys head to meet Zelensky after talks with Putin in Moscow
articles.title_zh: US envoys head to meet Zelensky after talks with Putin in Moscow
articles.content_orig:
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held a fresh round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest discussions aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
The pair are now flying to Dublin to meet Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Witkoff said a new round of trilateral talks had already been agreed with Putin.
But in a sign of further tension, Zelensky said on Thursday morning that Ukraine's military was again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
The peace talks in the Emirates were framed as being centred around European security arrangements in a post-war scenario, although a resolution to the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 still appears distant.
Comments by both President Vladimir Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Witkoff said that Europeans would join the next round of talks. "They are our partners and it's important to us that they take part," Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham had said that UK national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join Zelensky, Witkoff and Kushner for talks in Dublin, but Downing Street later said they had been delayed, meaning the national security adviser could no longer join.
Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side but added "some things" were already clear: "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going." He did not elaborate further.
Starshield was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use. Along with Starlink, it has come to play a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line. A similar issue with connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed and it remained unclear who had ordered the temporary restrictions.
Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".
Meanwhile, some of the longstanding roadblocks in the peace process were addressed during the US-Russia talks in the Kremlin.
The territorial issue continues to be a key point of contention, Putin said.
"For us there is only one line of demarcation: the line of the state border. Because then it will be clear that we are here, and you are there. As soon as we start discussing 'grey zones'… arguments immediately start and any agreements become unstable. And there will be no lasting peace."
He also suggested organising a humanitarian truce to allow for the evacuation of hundreds of civilians from a frontline area, on the model of last month's ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Putin suggested a similar five-day ceasefire for Kostyantynivka, a contested front-line Ukrainian city in the eastern region of Donetsk.
Kyiv disputes that Russia fully holds the town, and a truce could help Moscow's troops to make a final push to seize it.
"Considering that they brought in equipment and rotated troops in Oleshky under the guise of a humanitarian operation, it's clear what they want in Kostyantynivka," Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmitry Lytvyn told the BBC, adding that the details would need to be "clarified".
But at the core of this week's talks has been the issue of European security architecture. Earlier Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said it was "clear that the current system does not work."
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin and that decisions about their continent could be made without them.
Zelensky said he found the US approach of discussing a new European security order with Russia "a bit strange".
"It is a significant shift in the US position that the US has now taken on board the Russian demand that the European security architecture needs to be discussed and agreed upon in parallel with the Ukraine peace talks," said the Director of the Estonian Foreign Policy Institute Kristi Raik.
She said the Russians have a "long history" of wanting to revise European security architecture, intended as core principles "like sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principle that there is no use of force to some conflicts".
Russia "has long looked to reduced Nato presence on the Eastern flank and that… get some kind of veto rights in decisions concerning European security and defence," Raik said. "And that's where it gets even more difficult to imagine that there could be an agreement between the Europeans and the Russians."
On Thursday, Putin again repeated that the presence of foreign troops in Ukraine was "unacceptable" to Russia, and said Russia would like the Americans to engage with Europe "so that the Europeans can decide what they truly want: peace or war".
During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.
That position has now shifted for many as concern that decisions about the European continent could be made without European involvement.
Kushner also urged Europe to "identify one person to speak on their behalf" in the negotiations.
Top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas told the BBC's Newshour programme the presence of a European official at the next meeting showed the Kremlin had "now realised that Europe is a big player here because we are the ones who have been supporting Ukraine".
With financial pressures on European budgets, Kallas said it was "becoming harder to help Ukraine", but warned of the "the danger not only for the eastern flank of the European Union but actually for our whole continent" if Russian aggression was allowed to continue.
The Kremlin has not confirmed the make-up of next week's talks, and at the start of the meeting, Putin had indicated he didn't want European countries to play a full role. The Russians have long cited Europe's support for Kyiv as an obstacle to their involvement.
Speaking to Kushner and Witkoff, Putin said he was encouraging them "to work with your European allies so that they finally decide whether they want peace or war in Ukraine."

articles.title_orig: THC drink companies rush to sell inventory as Illinois ban takes effect
articles.title_zh: THC drink companies rush to sell inventory as Illinois ban takes effect
articles.content_orig:
Many hemp companies are shipping their remaining inventory to Wisconsin, Minnesota and Tennessee, which have different regulations
At midnight this morning in Illinois , hemp-derived THC drinks transformed from grocery store commodities into illegal narcotics, and manufacturers have been rushing to sell their inventory or ship it out of state.
Republicans tacked a last-minute provision on to last year’s spending bill that ended the government shutdown, banning all hemp-derived THC products, including the THC-infused alcohol alternatives sold at liquor stores and grocery stores . Under the new law, no container can have more than 0.4mg THC total.
In June, Illinois passed a state-level law intended to align with the federal ban, initially set to go into effect this month. While Congress delayed the federal ban until December, Illinois did not change its state-level effective date.
There has been some confusion around the Illinois ban because of a lawsuit filed last week by the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association, a hemp lobbying trade group that includes approximately 250 Illinois businesses. Some headlines suggested the lawsuit effectively paused the Illinois hemp ban until 19 November, but that pause only applies to businesses that sued .
The timing of the ban is unfortunate for Playdate, a non-alcoholic wine company that launched its first product, a THC-infused, NA rosé, less than two months ago. With less than two weeks to go before the ban, Playdate cofounders Sammy Dorf and Brian Ward were still unsure how to handle their remaining inventory. It’s possible the federal government will ultimately leave hemp-derived THC regulation to the states, mirroring their approach to medical and recreational cannabis.
Many hemp companies are strategically shipping their remaining inventory to Minnesota and Tennessee, which already have their own hemp regulations. After selling off Playdate wine at a steep discount, Dorf and Ward said they have less than a truckload left, which they’ll ship to states where they can still sell it. If the hemp ban remains in place, Ward and Dorf intend to shift their focus to plain NA wine, minus the THC.
Joe Chura, CEO and founder of Go Brewing in Naperville, Illinois , got into the business the other way around. Chura’s initial goal was to create the world’s first gluten-free, NA beer. He launched Easy Man, a THC-infused option, just last year, hoping to provide an alternative buzz without the health consequences of heavy drinking.
“Probably a month ago, we made our last batch,” Chura said. “We were planning another one that we ended up cancelling, because we didn’t want to get stuck with it.”
The last of the Easy Man left sold out on Friday, Chura added: “Had I known the demand would have been as great at the end, I probably would have made [the cancelled batch.] But it was cutting it close.”
Perfectly Dosed, a Chicago-based company that sells THC emulsions to beverage companies, didn’t have the option to dispense their remaining inventory in a fire sale, as they sell it to other companies in bulk. They had a metric ton of emulsion leftover, containing more than 100m milligrams of THC, according to cofounder and CEO Alexander Choi.
“We’re hopeful that more reasonable regulations will pass, and so we’d like our stuff closer to home than further,” Choi said. They shipped their metric ton of emulsion to Wisconsin.
Companies outside Illinois have another month to off-load their product. Joe Gerrity, CEO of Crescent Canna, has been selling beverages off to individual consumers by the pallet. He has some sense of who’s buying. “When someone’s buying thousands of dollars worth of product, you want to do some due diligence,” Gerrity said, adding that several former NBA players bought pallets.
One of the most difficult things about planning for the ban is the uncertainty around how it’s going to be implemented and enforced.
“It was hard for us to tell when distributors were going to stop selling our products, when retailers were going to ask them to be off the shelves,” Gerrity said.
While many in the industry don’t expect the federal government to strictly enforce the ban, alcohol distributors will probably still refuse THC beverages if there’s any possibility they could lose their license, Gerrity explained.
Gerrity is also working to figure out how to destroy inventory if necessary.
“You can’t just click a button and destroy thousands of pallets,” he said.
Choi, meanwhile, has been reformulating his emulsions to be chemically stable in case they need to be diluted to comply with federal regulations.
Despite the volatility of the industry, Chura said that he’s still hopeful that the bans will be reversed, and is even thinking about a THC beer compliant with federal regulations – that is, one that only contains 0.4mg of THC. It’s still unclear whether such a product would be legal.
Chura noted that when he first began making Easy Man, retailers would only buy high-dose products from him, but his online sales revealed his customers actually prefer lower doses. He imagines a beer with 0.4mg of THC could be appealing to people who like “having a few and knowing they still can be responsible”.

articles.title_zh: Is Microsoft Outlook down? Company investigates error reports from users
articles.content_orig:
The company posted about the disruptions on social media.
Microsoft reported issues with users' Exchange Online mailboxes and an issue with Microsoft Teams, according to posts on social media Thursday.
"We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas," the company wrote , after first reporting "users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America."
The company said it has identified a possible problem and is working on a fix.
Downdetector , which monitors outages, reported issues with both Microsoft Teams and Outlook, among other products on Thursday.
Regarding the issues with Microsoft Teams, the company followed up, writing, "Our mitigative actions have successfully restored service health and functionality."
Regarding the issues affecting Exchange Online mailboxes, the company added, "we've confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region."
The company continued to provide updates on the potential fix to the mailbox issue on Thursday, and added, "We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. We've paused all deployments, we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service."

articles.title_zh: Iran unveils new peace demand amid reports of 'shouting match' between Trump, Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s Assembly of Experts, the body tasked with overseeing Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, called Thursday for a review of Tehran’s membership in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and a revision of the country’s defense doctrine.
The assembly said the NPT review and defense doctrine revision had become an “inevitable necessity” and a public demand. It urged officials to address the demands under Khamenei’s guidance, according to a statement reported by IRGC-affiliated Tasnim News Agency .
The assembly also proposed establishing a wartime economic headquarters to counter economic warfare and issued a warning: “the unsuccessful enemies seek to test their ill-fated fortunes once again and launch another attack, they will certainly face an immediate and effective response from our heroic forces, without geographical limitations.”
The Saudi-led coalition intercepted and destroyed two Houthi drones targeting Riyadh and eastern Saudi Arabia on Thursday, coalition officials said.
“A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia was intercepted and destroyed in the Riyadh area,” coalition spokesman Col. Turki al-Malki said in a post on X .
The coalition also reported intercepting a second Houthi drone targeting Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province.
The interceptions came after the Houthis claimed to have targeted several sites in Saudi Arabia, including a Saudi Aramco facility in Riyadh.
Iran’s top security official warned Thursday that the IRGC Aerospace Force is prepared to deliver “new surprises on the battlefield” against the United States.
“The missile industry of the Islamic Republic of Iran stands as a proud symbol of faith, courage, initiative, and jihadi management,” he said in comments carried by Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim News Agency .
“It has evolved into one of Iran’s most vital instruments of deterrence and a steadfast pillar in safeguarding the independence and security of our beloved Iran.”
“Today, the IRGC Aerospace Force has made the wise directives and strategies of the Commander-in-Chief (of the Armed Forces) the guiding principle of its operations,” Rezaei added.
“The force stands firmly prepared for self-sacrifice and the creation of new surprises on the battlefield against the American-Zionist enemy,” Rezaei said.
The Houthis claimed Thursday to have launched drone and missile attacks targeting Saudi Aramco in Riyadh, an oil pipeline pumping station, a facility in Yanbu and military installations.
“Our armed forces have just targeted the Aramco company in Riyadh, the capital of the Saudi enemy, using a drone, and the operation successfully achieved its objective,” Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said in a post on X .
Saree also said Houthi forces also carried out two operations targeting Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure.
The first involved a drone attack on a pumping station along the kingdom’s east-west oil pipeline , a major route used to transport crude oil to the Red Sea. The second targeted an oil facility in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, according to Saree.
Saree also claimed a drone targeted a military cargo plane at Sharurah Airport, while a ballistic missile struck the Khamis Mushait Air Base.
President Donald Trump defended the war in Iran and said it will be over "soon" during his Veterans Day address on Wednesday.
Trump made the statement while speaking to a crowd of veterans and their families at Arlington National Cemetery. He highlighted the 1983 Iran-backed bombing of the U.S. Marine Corps barracks in Beirut and argued that Iran has been at war with the U.S. for decades.
"America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. They should have been taken care of a long time ago," Trump said.
"And it was just about time somebody fought back. All of us fought back. We fought back, and we fought back. We won. Now the question is when we want to end. We must have a total victory. Not a 93% victory. It's going to be total," he continued.
Trump noted that of the roughly seven months of conflict, "only a few weeks were active fighting," but he acknowledged the casualties America sustained.
"We lost 18 beautiful souls," Trump said. "When this conflict is over, and it will be soon, the entire world will be much safer, a better place, more peaceful place and a place without the kind of danger that we had to suffer."
Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have shied away from plans to re-escalate the conflict with Iran following the midterm elections.
President Donald Trump said Thursday that he has asked Vice President JD Vance to focus his "complete and total attention" on alleged widespread corruption and crime in Democrat-led cities and states, accusing blue state leaders of allowing billions of dollars to be stolen each month.
In a Truth Social post, Trump singled out Minnesota, California and Illinois as examples of states he claims are plagued by corruption and mismanagement, arguing that cracking down on the alleged criminal activity could help balance the federal budget.
"I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.," Trump wrote.
"The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters," he continued. "Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month."
Trump did not provide specific examples in his post of how billions of dollars are allegedly being stolen each month.
Vance already leads the White House's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, which Trump established through a March 16 executive order aimed at combating fraud, waste and abuse in federally funded benefit programs.
The task force is charged with coordinating federal efforts to strengthen eligibility verification, prevent improper payments and identify suspected fraud in government benefit programs.
The executive order also identified Minnesota, California and Illinois among states where the administration alleged widespread fraud or vulnerabilities in government benefit programs.
This is an excerpt from an article by Fox News' Stephen Sorace.
Three suspected Iran-backed terrorists plotted an attack on a British air base housing American troops using vans carrying barrels of fuel, according to a federal indictment unsealed Tuesday by the Justice Department (DOJ).
The eight-count superseding indictment charges Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani with terrorism-related offenses tied to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Kata'ib Hizballah.
Prosecutors say the suspects targeted RAF Fairford in England, where U.S. military aircraft and personnel were stationed.
"Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a news release.
According to the indictment, Al-Hassani directed associates in the United Kingdom to conduct surveillance of RAF Fairford in August, paying one individual to record video of the base's perimeter.
The suspects' associates later obtained three vans and barrels of fuel, researched chemical accelerants and purchased metal objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel, prosecutors said. They also disguised the vans with commercial decals to resemble vehicles belonging to fuel delivery and swimming pool supply businesses.
On Sept. 26, Al-Hassani allegedly directed associates to drive the three vans toward the base. At least two encountered a security roadblock and were unable to proceed. British authorities recovered all three vehicles and arrested their occupants the following morning.

articles.title_orig: US home sales fall to lowest level since 2010 as mortgage rates soar
articles.title_zh: US home sales fall to lowest level since 2010 as mortgage rates soar
articles.content_orig:
Home sales fell to their lowest since 2010, a new report shows, in large part due to high mortgage rates. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption
The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.
Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.
"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com . "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."
The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.
In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.
Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.
Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.
"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.

articles.title_orig: Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence
articles.title_zh: Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence
articles.content_orig:
After this week’s Carbon availability , Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”
Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:
“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”
In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”
In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”
Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”
Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:
…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.
Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.
This naming scheme is not the most intuitive.
In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”
To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.
For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.
Hydrogen is available in Antigravity for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.
For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

articles.title_orig: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
After being moored along Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary this week, the 120-metre-long (400-foot-long) cargo ship Karin set sail for Russia.
The vessel was laden with a bulk cargo of white powder that can be forged into weapons which are vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine .
Alumina, a key ingredient in aluminium, goes into products from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones.
A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland operates as Europe’s biggest alumina refinery, regularly sending shiploads of the substance directly to St Petersburg and other Russian ports.
Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy . That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where experts say some ends up in weapons.
“The material is clearly ending up in military supplies," said Irish politician Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party.
“It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.”
Ireland faces mounting calls to halt the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders.
Irish government minister Niall Collins said that "there’s absolutely no evidence" the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to publish the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments.
Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.”
Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives.
The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska, a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the US and Australian governments.
While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic.
The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia.
These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories – one in Australia, the other in Ukraine – stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40 per cent, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU.
Roughly 17 per cent of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU.
An investigation by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times , published earlier this year, found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors.
“Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU.
Standing next to Irish President Micheál Martin in Dublin in June, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said: “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.”
Mr Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.”
Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it is not, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.
The Irish government has not published its findings, but it handed them to the European Commission, which drafts EU sanctions packages.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan said there is little doubt that “the alumina goes to smelters in Russia who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex”.
“I’ve read the government report. Personally, I think there’s no doubt the investigative journalists got it right,” he said in October in Dublin at a meeting organized by the Institute of International and European Affairs.
The European Parliament in July passed a non-binding motion calling for a ban on alumina exports to Russia. But alumina was not included in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia that month. The EU’s executive European Commission, which draws up sanctions packages, is now sounding out member nations about the Irish alumina exports. Sanctions must be agreed upon unanimously by the bloc's 27 countries.
A commission spokesperson said in July that the bloc’s sanctions policy was “a delicate balance” between thwarting Russia’s war effort and limiting “negative impacts” on EU member nations, “especially considering that alumina is a critical raw material”.
Supporters of the plant point to the hundreds of jobs it provides, and to its role as a key source of alumina for European countries. Keeping supply lines open is especially important because of the chokehold on cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Mr Collins, who represents County Limerick in Ireland's parliament, said Ireland has been "hugely resolute in our support for the Ukrainians, and Ukraine hasn’t provided any evidence that Aughinish is doing anything adverse”.
Opposition politicians remain skeptical. Ms Bacik's left-of-center Labour Party supports a temporary nationalisation of the refinery, similar to when Ireland seized banks in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. She says the refinery can ban exports to Russia and find other eager customers in Europe.
“We need to see much stronger action being taken on this from other EU countries if the Irish government isn’t willing to do the right thing here,” she said.
In Foynes, the wind-swept port town beside the plant, many work at Aughinish or know someone who does. But some locals have mixed feelings.
“It's too big a business for them to close it down,” said retired docker Joe Hanlon. “Too much employment for the government to get involved.”
But he said “of course they should”, if Ireland wants “to stop the war on Ukraine”.

articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the Health Ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday.
The strike hit a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, with medical staff and patients among those killed, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, health officials said. The Israeli military said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants.
The strike — the latest despite an ongoing U.S.-backed ceasefire — shattered ceilings and left debris strewn across wards inside the hospital, which is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza after the destruction of Israel’s yearslong military assault.
Palestinian surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira was among those killed, the Health Ministry said. He was featured in the 2026 documentary “American Doctor,” which followed three American doctors helping to provide medical care in Gaza.
Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, head of the surgery department at Nasser Hospital, said there was no “notice, warning or anything” before the hospital was attacked. “Suddenly, there was fire and shelling and walls were brought down instantly,” he said.
He said he was not aware of any “resistance fighters or combatants present — only a medical team treating patients.”
NBC News also spoke with two surgeons who said they were in the hospital when the missile struck after traveling to Gaza from the U.K. earlier this month to assist with medical care.
Both Dr. Goher Rahbour, a consultant general and colorectal surgeon, and Dr. Stephan Verborg, a limb reconstruction surgeon, said they were also not aware of any warning from the Israeli military before the strike, which hit the hospital shortly after midnight.
“I heard the impact and I felt the explosion because the whole hospital shook,” Verborg said in a phone interview Thursday. He said he was about 15 to 20 meters away from the point of impact, adding: “You could smell the smoke. You could see the dust.”
Rahbour said he had been operating with Abu Shaira, whom he described as a “lovely” and “affable” person, earlier that day. He said they had been laughing and joking together Wednesday evening in the hours just before the Palestinian surgeon was killed.
Both doctors had traveled to Gaza early this month through the organization IDEALS, a U.K. charity seeking to provide sustainable humanitarian aid to regions affected by conflict or natural disasters. They said they had not seen any indication of a Hamas presence in the hospital.
Tributes were paid to Abu Shaira. “Dr. Rizq was at the hospital during the entire war,” Dr. Mohammed Zaqout, director general of the Health Ministry in Gaza, could be seen telling a crowd of mourners, surrounding a body covered in a shroud, in a video captured for NBC News on Thursday. “He didn’t abandon his duties for even one day.”
Nasser Hospital said a 13-year-old boy, identified as Jihad Naeem Muhammad Abu Tilikh, was also among those killed.
The Israeli military and the Israel Security Agency said they struck a senior Hamas member, along with other militants, who they said had “advanced” attacks from the hospital in the southern Gaza Strip overnight. In a later statement, they identified the senior member as Muhammad Abu Ismail, who they said served as the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade and had also been responsible for holding hostages in Gaza.
The IDF and ISA said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command center” and stored weapons and conducted interrogations and torture from within the medical complex. They shared photos of weapons alleged to have been found within the complex.
The IDF and ISA said steps had been taken to “mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.” They also later said “advance warnings were issued to the population.” The IDF said it was looking into reports that medical workers,  including Abu Shaira, and patients were killed.
One woman, Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza, said her brother, Khaled Abu Anza, was killed in the strike, with Nasser Hospital separately confirming his death.
A number of media outlets, including Israeli media outlet Ynet , reported that a commander in Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade of that same name was killed in the strike. Asked to confirm that and whether he was directly targeted, the IDF said it would get back on the matter.
Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza did not directly identify her brother, 53, as a Hamas member, but said she believed he was targeted. He had been at the hospital for physical therapy after undergoing surgery, she said.
“He did not come to the hospital to engage in combat or resistance. He came for medical treatment,” she said.
Hamas condemned the allegations that it was using the hospital for military operations as “lies of the criminal enemy” and called the attack a “war crime.”
Hospitals have protected status under international law, but they have been heavily targeted under Israel’s yearslong offensive in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating within medical facilities, a charge the militant group has denied.
The overnight attack was not the first time that Nasser Hospital itself has been targeted.
In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double tap Israeli strik e that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The deadly attack sparked international outrage.
Of Gaza’s 37 hospitals, just two are considered to be “fully functioning,” while 18 are partially functioning and 17 are considered nonfunctioning after much of the enclave’s healthcare system was devastated under Israel’s offensive, according to data published by the World Health Organization.
Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached in October of last year.
More than 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the enclave. Israel says four of its ⁠soldiers have ​been killed in that time.
Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
More than 74,600 people, including thousands of children, have been killed overall in Gaza since Israel launched its offensive in the enclave following the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed and around 250 taken hostage.
In a statement, Medical Aid for Palestinians, which supports several departments at Nasser Hospital, said the overnight attack was “yet another indication that the so-called ‘ceasefire’ has brought neither safety nor an end to Israel’s attacks on Gaza’s healthcare system.”
The latest strikes come as Palestinians contend with heavy rains and desperate conditions in the enclave as the colder months set in, prompting a fresh wave of outcry over the lack of progress in advancing the peace deal between Israel and Hamas.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq wavers as traders weigh Nvidia CEO exit, AMD climbs: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq wavers as traders weigh Nvidia CEO exit, AMD climbs: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite fluctuated on Thursday as investors assessed the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , betting it would not derail the whole AI trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq was last down 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline. The S&P 500 fell 0.1%.
Selling pressure on Nvidia eased a bit, with the stock last down 5%. The shares were down double digits at one point after the company announced that Huang had resigned and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. This comes after Huang reportedly had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Investors moved into competitors of Nvidia, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom , helping to bolster the market. AMD shares were up 4%, while Broadcom gained 5%.
Hyperscalers Microsoft and Alphabet — key buyers of Nvidia chips and leaders of the AI rally — also increased.
"This is a golden opportunity for Amazon, for Google, for AMD, for Broadcom, for OpenAI and Anthropic, who are hiring chip experts to help them design their own chips," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management.
"Nvidia's fate as one company is one thing, but this AI revolution is way bigger than that," he also said. "If Nvidia falls from grace and their chips are no longer the best, and AMDs are better or Google's are better, then people will switch over and buy them. The demand for the chips is not is not going down."
There was a sense from investors that perhaps Huang's exit was a capitulation event for the AI trade with Nvidia's stock down by more than 25% the past one month as this scandal was unfolding.
"We are sticking with the thesis that technology stocks bottomed last week," said Tom Lee, the head of research at Fundstrat, in a note Thursday. Huang's departure "does not change our view."
Stocks outside of technology such as JPMorgan and Eli Lilly traded higher as well.
Stephanie Link said Thursday she sold her Nvidia following Jensen Huang's resignation from his post as CEO, with the investor moving into another artificial intelligence play: Micron Technology .
"The fundamentals are very, very strong at [Nvidia], and I expect the quarter next week to be very good with 300 billion in free cash flow next year," Link, the chief investment strategist at Hightower Advisors, said on CNBC's " Halftime Report ." "But, this stock is not going to trade on fundamentals ... for a while because you have the overhang of the investigations of leadership changes of potential departures."
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Nvidia shares were trading down 4% on Thursday after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker.
The stock hovered just under $4 trillion in market cap, after paring steeper losses earlier in the day of more than 10%. Nvidia has closed above the market cap benchmark since July 2025.
Read the full story here .
Paul Meeks says he's buying Nvidia shares with "both hands" despite CEO Jensen Huang's resignation , because the decline amid this unfolding scandal has brought the stock down to "stupid" valuation levels.
The Freedom Capital head of technology research noted that the stock is trading at just 10 times fiscal 2028 earnings estimates after Thursday's decline.
Nvidia shares are off 20% in November alone, pressured by the scandal unfolding.
"I think that the actual announcement of his resignation is a market-clearing event," said Meeks.
CNBC Pro subscribers can learn more about Meeks' other key points here .
Even as Nvidia shares remained lower following CEO Jensen Huang's resignation , the broader market rose as investors moved past the announcement.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite , both of which began Thursday's session lower, rose 0.2% and 0.1%, respectively.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 138 points, or 0.3%.
Sales of existing homes fell to their lowest level in more than 16 years during October, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday.
A decline of 5.5% brought the seasonally adjusted annualized rate down to 3.75 million during a month that saw mortgage rates continue to climb, putting pressure on an already beleaguered housing market. The total was the lowest since August 2010.
"Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun. "Based on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline."
Nvidia shares are seeing huge volume as the stock drops following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang .
The chipmaker saw more than 373 million shares traded amid the selling pressure. That's above the stock's 30-day average of 144.4 million.
The stock was last down more than 5%.
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said Thursday she doesn't see the need for aggressive interest rate increases ahead.
While Hammack still supports rate hikes as the Fed struggles to get inflation back to its 2% target, she advocated for a gradual approach that the economy can adapt to more easily.
"I think we need to move rates higher to get to a restrictive stance of policy to bring inflation back down to 2%. My view is that if we go steadily in smaller increments, more frequent, smaller rises, it's easier for businesses and households to manage around that," she sad. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements."
Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller raised the specter of a half-point hike at the December meeting if the inflation data comes in worse than anticipated. However, Hammack said she doesn't think that's necessary, at least for now.
"If we get behind the curve, and I don't think we're behind the curve today, but if we get behind the curve, then that might be something that we need to consider," she said. "So I'll certainly have an open mind walking into that December meeting."
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Thursday's session in the red.
The broad market index fell 0.8% shortly after the opening bell, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq declined 1.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 108 points, or 0.2%.
Shares of Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices gained about 3% each in premarket trading after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia.
The company's chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim chief.
Nvidia shares were last down about 10%.
For more, follow along with our live updates of Nvidia and Jensen Huang here .
Initial jobless claims showed a modest pop last week after hovering around their lowest levels since the late 1960s.
First-time filings for unemployment benefits totaled a seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ending Nov. 7, a gain of 9,000 from the prior period and higher than the Dow Jones consensus for 195,000, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
Continuing claims, which run a week behind, fell 20,000 to just below 1.7 million.
Nebius shares plummeted in the premarket on Thursday after the neocloud's third-quarter revenue topped analysts' expectations, but its guidance disappointed investors.
The stock was last down almost 16%. That's after it rose more than 15% in Wednesday's regular session.
— Jordan Novet and Sean Conlon

Analysts said his ouster could lead to a 20%-plus decline in the shares with the uncertainty that would follow overhanging the stock a bit longer after that.

articles.title_orig: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
articles.title_zh: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new retirement account contribution limits for 2027.
In its release on Thursday, the agency increased the 401(k) employee deferral limit to $25,500 next year, up from $24,500 in 2026. The change applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s and most 457 plans, along with the federal Thrift Savings Plan.
The IRS also unveiled 2027 catch-up contribution limits for savers age 50 and older, new individual retirement account savings limits and higher income thresholds for Roth IRA contributions.
Starting in 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution limit will rise to $8,500 for savers 50 and older, up from $8,000 in 2026. But investors aged 60 to 63 can instead save an extra $11,750, based on changes enacted via Secure 2.0 . That figure is up $500 from 2026.
Both amounts are in addition to the $25,500 deferral limit for 2027.
The 2027 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, unchanged from 2026, the IRS announced. IRA catch-up contributions for investors age 50 and older will be $1,100, the same as 2026.
The announcement comes one week after the agency released dozens of other inflation adjustments for 2027, including federal income tax brackets , higher capital gains brackets , estate and gift tax exemptions and provisions impacting families, among others.
In 2025, only 14% of participants maxed out their 401(k)s , according to Vanguard's 2026 How America Saves report, which was based on data from more than 1,300 qualified plans and nearly 5 million participants. The average combined savings rate, including employer deposits, was an estimated 12.1%, according to the same report.
"Before worrying about contribution limits, make sure you're capturing your full employer match," said Sean Michael Pearson, a certified financial planner with Ameriprise Financial Services in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania.
During the second quarter of 2026, about 19% of employees weren't deferring enough to 401(k)s to receive their company's full matching contribution, according to a Fidelity analysis of 27,300 corporate plans and nearly 26 million participants.
Vanguard suggests saving 12% to 15% of your pay per year, including employer contributions, depending on your income. But only one-quarter of 401(k) participants deferred more than 10% of earnings in 2025, according to Vanguard's report.
If you plan to max out your 401(k) for 2027, you should change your savings rate in December so it's active by your first January paycheck, experts say. The update could take one or two pay periods to go into effect.
The "most important habit" is consistently increasing your 401(k) savings rate over time, according to Pearson.
For example, if you bump 401(k) contributions by 1% every year, "you may barely notice the difference in your paycheck, but the long-term impact can be substantial," he said.
In 2025, about 27% of 401(k) plans automatically increased employee deferrals over time, known as "auto-escalation," according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America's yearly survey of 401(k)s . The nonprofit trade organization's survey included 753 plans.
The vast majority of plans with auto-escalation, 69%, boosted deferrals by 1% per year, the Plan Sponsor Council of America found.

articles.title_orig: Here's what Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees
articles.title_zh: Here's what Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees
articles.content_orig:
On the heels of founder Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia , new interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sent emails to employees Thursday expressing gratitude and optimism for the future.
CNBC obtained copies of the emails from a source familiar with the matter, who said Jones sent the first email and Kress replied shortly after.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation
"The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication," Kress wrote in her email.
The term Estaff is commonly used to refer to executive staff, the group of direct reports to C-suite executives at a company. Nvidia will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PST, her email said.
Board chair Jones took a similar tone in his email, and praised Kress as "a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy."
"The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you," Jones wrote.
Below are the staff emails obtained by CNBC on Thursday.
I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy.
The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.
This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT.
We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let's move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company.
Thank you for all you do, Colette
I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board.
As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you.
Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence.
The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.
The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette's leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA.
Harvey Jones Chair, NVIDIA Board of Directors

articles.content_orig:
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., discusses the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, the need for an investigations and the national security implications if China gains access to U.S. chips on 'Varney & Co.'
President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang as the head of Nvidia following Huang's abrupt resignation amid scrutiny of his personal conduct and potential national security concerns.
"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The president's endorsement comes as Nvidia faces a leadership shake-up following Huang's departure from the artificial intelligence chipmaker he co-founded in 1993.
NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG RESIGNS AMID INVESTIGATION INTO RELATIONSHIP WITH ALLEGED CHINESE SPY
Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., and President Donald Trump. (Graeme Sloan/Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg)
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO on Thursday while its board searches for a permanent successor, considering candidates from both inside and outside the company.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Sept. 2, 2026, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images)
Cook stepped down as Apple's CEO in September after 15 years at the helm and now serves as the iPhone maker's executive chairman. Trump did not indicate whether Cook had expressed interest in taking the helm at Nvidia.
Huang's resignation followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
The allegations raised questions about whether the longtime technology executive could have been targeted by Chinese intelligence, given Nvidia's central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and ongoing U.S.-China tensions over advanced chips.
No evidence has been publicly established that Huang disclosed confidential information or that the woman obtained Nvidia secrets. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto)
The reported relationship has fueled concerns about potential foreign intelligence efforts to gain access to sensitive information involving one of America's most strategically important technology companies. However, no evidence has been publicly established that Huang disclosed confidential information or that the woman obtained Nvidia secrets.

Trump had previously defended Huang, saying Monday that he believed the executive's account that he was unaware of the woman's alleged intelligence ties.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US FDA shelves commissioner's voucher program for speedy drug reviews, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US FDA shelves commissioner's voucher program for speedy drug reviews, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program is coming to an end. That is, companies can still submit applications, but if they do, they won’t go anywhere. That’s according to six anonymous sources who spoke with Reuters .
As Heidi Overton’s Senate confirmation for FDA commissioner hangs in the balance, awaiting a vote from the now lame-duck legislative body, the FDA has shelved the CNPV program , which was launched by former Commissioner Marty Makary in July 2025 to shorten review times for certain products aligning with national priorities.
Of the 22 drugs that secured a voucher, 12 have been approved since the program’s inception in June 2025, according to Reuters , including five since Makary’s departure in May.
There have been no new vouchers awarded since Makary left, however, and an executive council of political appointees that oversaw drug reviews “has gone dormant,” according to internal documents reviewed by Reuters .
Neither of the most recent approvals for CNPV-holder—Revolution Medicines’ pancreatic cancer drug Rasonque and Merck’s cholesterol pill Lipfendra —were vetted by the executive council, Reuters reported.
Companies were told by agency leadership that the FDA is not moving forward with the CNPV program but is keeping applications open, one source told Reuters . When companies submit them, however, they don’t advance, according to this source.
There has been no official guidance from the FDA on the program, “nor is it clear the extent to which this may impact companies with an existing CNPV rather than new applicants to the program, ” RBC Capital Markets analysts wrote to investors on Thursday morning.
“FDA’s commitment to its core mission remains unchanged, and work under the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher (CNPV) Pilot Program is ongoing,” an FDA spokesperson told BioSpace in an email. “FDA career staff continues to evaluate applications granted a CNPV and meet commitments for accelerated review and enhanced engagement as we assess best practices learned under this pilot program.”
Two CNPV holders, Compass Pathways and Usona Institute , have recently submitted applications for their psychedelic therapeutics, COMP360 for treatment-resistant depression and PSIL201 for major depressive disorder, respectively.
“While it is not fully clear how these updates may impact COMP360, this may add incremental risk to timelines,” RBC said. But the analysts noted that COMP360 has breakthrough status and should thus be eligible for priority review, the analysts added, so the impact from any change in timing “should be manageable.”
RBC remained positive on Compass’ shot at a regulatory greenlight, saying they “do not see added risk on an approval (est. 85% PoS) given CMPS’s strong data which stands on its own and should clear a traditional FDA review.”
News about the CNPV program’s possible closure comes as industry watchers are debating Overton’s chances of passing an upcoming Senate vote to become FDA commissioner.
“While a vote on Dr. Overton’s nomination has been scheduled for Nov. 18, there is clearly uncertainty over whether a majority can be reached amongst members present at the vote given impending changes in the committee members,” William Blair wrote on Thursday after a conversation with representatives from LMH Strategic Solutions on the implications of the recent midterm elections for the healthcare and life sciences sector.
“Should Dr. Overton not pass the committee vote, there could also be changes in the current acting commissioner, with news outlets reporting that Sara Brenner could return as acting commissioner in 2027,” the analysts wrote.
During a Senate hearing in late September, U.S. senators grilled Overton on her ability to “stand up” to President Donald Trump.
“This committee needs to know whether you’ll be radically honest, whether you will use your authority to stand up for sound science and protect children’s health,” outgoing Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee chairman Bill Cassidy (R-LA) said during hearing.
HPS Group President and regulatory consultant Steven Grossman cast doubt on Overton’s chances of securing the position.
“Controversial nominations rarely advance during a lame-duck session,” Grossman wrote in a piece for MedPage Today last Friday.
“Given the White House affiliation with Heidi Overton, MD, PhD, and her weaker credentials compared to her predecessors, I see no way senators would confirm her as FDA commissioner in the lame-duck session,” Grossman continued. “Obviously, her odds would be even worse next year with a Democratic-led Senate.”
